title: Kullervo: The Cheat-Cake
subtitle: An insult to a knife sparks retaliation

learningObjectives.text: What does breaking the knife mean?

knife.author: Elias Lönnrot, compiler and editor
knife.locator: Rune XXXIII · Kullervo and the Cheat-cake; Rune XXXIII · Kullervo and the Cheat-cake, normalized characters 2870-3163
knife.excerpt: This, the blade that I hold sacred, This the one thing that I honor, Relic of my mother’s people! On the stone within this oat-loaf, On this cheat-cake of the hostess, I my precious knife have broken. How shall I repay this insult, How avenge this woman’s malice, What the wages for deception?
knife.note: Verbatim English verse translated by John Martin Crawford from Lönnrot's nineteenth-century compilation of oral poetry; not a transcript of one ancient or single oral witness.

narrativeBlocks.title: The slave who hates his life
narrativeBlocks.body: Kullervo, sold into slavery as a child, grows up sullen and wronged — the Kalevala's tragic, violent anti-hero.

narrativeBlocks.title: The cheat-cake
narrativeBlocks.body: Sent out with a cake for his meal, he cuts into it — and finds a stone baked inside, placed there by the wife who hates him. The cheat-cake breaks his knife.

narrativeBlocks.title: The knife that was everything
narrativeBlocks.body: The knife was his only heirloom — his father's gift and his one possession. Breaking it on the stone is the last wrong his life can bear.

narrativeBlocks.title: The revenge and the reckoning
narrativeBlocks.body: In rage he conjures wolves and bears to tear the wife's herd — and then kills her — then kills himself, the poem's darkest arc of revenge and consequence.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why the cheat-cake matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The Kalevala's Kullervo is the tragedy of the wronged made violent: a small cruelty — a stone in a cake — is the thing that finally breaks him.
